vignette: He is sixty years old, raised in a Southeast Asian household where resilience was practiced in quiet endurance, standing in the dimly lit corridor of the hotel's east wing, listening to the distant hum of the exhaust fans. Ten years ago, during a routine winter maintenance cycle, the main pressure valve on the building's original heating plant ruptured. He was the last to leave the boiler room, double-checking the gauges, when the valve failed completely. A plume of chloramine and volatile organic compounds rolled across the concrete floor. By the time he stumbled into the stairwell, coughing and with a metallic taste coating his throat, the air had turned thick and pale. The emergency crews treated his lungs, cleared him within three weeks, and sent him back to the front desk. He told himself it was just an industrial accident. But the hotel itself slowly becomes the source of his anxiety. He begins tracking the ventilation systems with an intensity that alarms his maintenance supervisor. The scent of quaternary ammonium cleaners makes his chest tighten, and he starts rerouting housekeeping schedules to avoid the lower levels. When guests complain about a faint chemical odor in their rooms, he insists on inspecting the ductwork himself, often kneeling in the crawl spaces until his knees ache, convinced that any microscopic leak will resurrect the gas. He sleeps in the upper-floor suites, with the windows cracked and a portable HEPA unit running beside the bed. He wakes at the slightest draft, heart pounding, hands checking the digital air quality monitor on his nightstand. The numbers must stay in the green. They have to stay in the green. His occupation is woven into his symptoms. During morning operational briefings, he watches the maintenance lead unpack a new bottle of industrial degreaser. His pulse quickens. He abruptly changes the subject to seasonal occupancy targets, his pen tapping a staccato rhythm against the ledger. His colleagues notice how he has stopped eating lunch in the staff cafeteria, preferring to work through the midday rush in his office with the door shut. He reads every safety data sheet on his tablet, cross-referencing ingredients, his mind circling the same quiet terror: Is the air safe? Is it still in the walls? He has stopped delegating filter replacements. He orders them himself, in bulk, storing them in the climate-controlled archive, counting boxes like provisions for a siege. At home, his partner, Linh, tries to maintain their routine. She opens the kitchen windows in the evening, but he follows her, turning the thermostat down to halt any airflow, then sits rigidly at the table, arms folded, listening to the refrigerator cycle on. He loves her, but the space between them feels heavy, as though the room itself is holding its breath. When she reaches for his hand, flashbacks surge unbidden-the chlorine sting, the way the ceiling tiles warped, the suffocating weight in his chest. He pulls away, not out of rejection, but out of a sudden, overwhelming need to control the temperature of the air around him. He avoids coastal trips where the damp, salt-heavy air triggers the same respiratory panic. He stays behind at the properties, walking the perimeter at dusk, watching the exhaust stacks vent into the sky, waiting for a sign that the atmosphere has finally cleared. His boots scuff the pavement, his breath steady but shallow, measuring each inhale against the quiet hope that it tastes like nothing at all.
